deps.helpBranchBody: Each repository is cloned at the branch saved on its registration (Repositories → the branch chip); repositories with no branch saved are read at the provider's default branch. The scope card shows the resolved branch per repository and can override it for a single run.
deps.helpEngineBody: The audit itself never calls an LLM. The engine picker (next to Run audit, or in the AI report card after a run) chooses who writes the executive REPORT over the facts: your workspace's review-profile API model (e.g. Gemini, with temperature) or Claude Code via the connected subscription.
deps.helpFixBody: Pick a repo in the findings filter → “Fix from here” opens an agent session pre-filled with the exact package list, target versions and CVE ids. Targets are the LOWEST version that clears every advisory on a package, not the latest release — a bigger jump is more breaking change for no extra security. The agent updates and verifies; Finish & push makes the branch.
deps.helpIntro: Facts are collected deterministically — no LLM can hallucinate a version or a CVE. The model (optional) only writes the analysis report.
deps.helpS1: Scan: each scoped repo's local clone — manifests (package.json, requirements.txt, pyproject.toml incl. Poetry, go.mod, Cargo.toml) AND lock files, so dependencies-of-dependencies are covered too. Repos without a clone are listed as skipped (press “index now” first).
deps.helpS2: Vulnerabilities: the ecosystem's own auditor first (pip-audit, npm/pnpm/yarn audit, govulncheck, cargo audit, composer audit, bundler-audit) — it resolves the full tree. Anything it can't cover falls back to OSV.dev, and every gap is listed under “Coverage & sources”.
deps.helpS3: Vulnerabilities: OSV.dev (Google's open vulnerability DB) batch query per package@version — each advisory carries severity, CVE and the fixed-in release.
deps.helpS4: Recommendations are rule-based: update now (vulnerable, fix exists) / safe update (patch-minor) / plan major / ok.
deps.helpS5: Runs as a background job (visible in Operations → Job queue); this page polls the progress phases live.
deps.hygieneDesc: Problems no vulnerability database reports: a lock file that disagrees with the manifest, code that runs at install time, dependencies from outside the registry, and names that imitate popular packages. Kept apart from CVEs on purpose.

alertGuide.title: Set up alerts and notifications
alertGuide.subtitle: Bring production problems in from your monitoring, and send finished reviews out to your team's chat.
alertGuide.twoHalves: Two halves that meet at a binding. Alerts arriving here go out to your chat channels — and so do finished reviews — but only where a binding says so: channel plus event plus minimum severity. Pick alert_received for what lands on this page, review_complete for reviews, or “any event” for both. Without a binding nothing is sent.
alertGuide.inboundIntro: Create the ingest URL in the card above first — it does not exist until you press the button, and the part after the dot is a secret. Anything that can POST JSON can use it.
alertGuide.in.grafana.title: Grafana
alertGuide.in.grafana.s1: Alerting → Contact points → Add contact point, Integration: Webhook.
alertGuide.in.grafana.s2: Paste the ingest URL into the URL field and save.
alertGuide.in.grafana.s3: Alerting → Notification policies: route the rules you care about to that contact point.
alertGuide.in.grafana.s4: On each alert rule add a label repo = owner/name. Celmis reads it (falling back to service) to pre-select the repository for “Fix from here”.
alertGuide.in.curl.title: Anything else — plain JSON
alertGuide.in.curl.s1: POST a JSON object to the ingest URL. No signature or header is needed; the URL is the credential.
alertGuide.in.curl.s2: title is required — a payload without one is accepted with HTTP 202 and stores nothing. body, severity (info, warning, error, critical) and repo are optional.
alertGuide.in.curl.s3: Alertmanager's own webhook format works too: an alerts array is read as one alert per entry.
alertGuide.outboundIntro: Get a webhook URL from the chat product, then register it as a channel. The Kind you pick decides the message format, so it has to match where the URL came from.
alertGuide.out.slack.title: Slack
alertGuide.out.slack.s1: api.slack.com/apps → Create New App → From scratch. Name it and pick the workspace.
alertGuide.out.slack.s2: Left menu → Incoming Webhooks → turn “Activate Incoming Webhooks” on.
alertGuide.out.slack.s3: Add New Webhook to Workspace → choose the channel → Allow.
alertGuide.out.slack.s4: Copy the URL (https://hooks.slack.com/services/…). It is a secret — anyone holding it can post to that channel.
alertGuide.out.slack.s5: In Celmis: Settings → Notification channels → New channel, Kind “Slack”, paste the URL, Add.
alertGuide.out.discord.title: Discord
alertGuide.out.discord.s1: Hover the target channel → gear icon (Edit Channel) → Integrations → Webhooks.
alertGuide.out.discord.s2: New Webhook, rename it if you like, then Copy Webhook URL.
alertGuide.out.discord.s3: The URL (https://discord.com/api/webhooks/…) is a secret and needs no further permissions.
alertGuide.out.discord.s4: In Celmis: Settings → Notification channels → New channel, Kind “Discord”, paste the URL, Add.
alertGuide.out.googlechat.title: Google Chat
alertGuide.out.googlechat.s1: Open the space → click the space name at the top → Apps & integrations → Webhooks.
alertGuide.out.googlechat.s2: Add webhook, give it a name, Save.
alertGuide.out.googlechat.s3: Copy the URL (https://chat.googleapis.com/…), which carries a key and a token — treat it as a secret.
alertGuide.out.googlechat.s4: In Celmis: Settings → Notification channels → New channel, Kind “Google Chat”, paste the URL, Add.
alertGuide.bindingWarning: A channel on its own never delivers anything. After adding it, press Test to confirm the URL works, then create a binding — channel plus event plus minimum severity, with the repo left blank to cover the whole workspace. Without a binding the channel stays silent forever.

webhooks.title: Connect auto-review
webhooks.subtitle: Turning auto-review on for a repository is only half of it — the provider still has to be told where to send pull request events, and both sides need the same secret.
webhooks.whyNotPolling: Why not just let Celmis check for new pull requests?
webhooks.whyNotPollingBody: Polling reads your GitHub notification inbox rather than the repository's pull requests. Fine-grained tokens (github_pat_…) cannot access that endpoint at all — it answers 403 — and GitHub never notifies you about your own pull requests, so one you opened yourself is never picked up. A webhook has neither limitation.

drift.subtitle: {count} value(s) changed here and still hardcoded elsewhere. Checked across {repos} repositories by reading them — no model involved.
drift.whyProven: Why is this separate from the review comments?
drift.whyProvenBody: Everything here was found by reading files: the value, the file it was removed from, and each place it still appears with the line and the line's text. You can agree or disagree in seconds. The review comments below are a model's judgement — often right, but not checkable at a glance, so they are kept apart rather than mixed into one list.
deps.whichExportBody: The documents above are for reading — the same audit as Word, Markdown or PDF. The SBOM is the CycloneDX inventory procurement asks for by name. The evidence pack is what an audit is filed with: the SBOMs, every finding, a timeline of runs and a sha256 of each file, so the archive can be shown not to have been edited afterwards.
onboarding.proof.title: See your first proven finding
onboarding.proof.body: Run the dependency audit. It needs no LLM key and reports only what it can prove — a lock file that disagrees with its manifest, a package that runs a script at install. The SBOM comes out of the same run.
onboarding.proof.started: Audit started — it takes a few minutes
onboarding.proof.needRepo: Add a repository in step 4 first — there is nothing to audit yet.
onboarding.proof.whyProven: A deterministic check, not a model's judgement: open the file at that line and see for yourself.
onboarding.proof.allClean: Nothing to flag: no lock drift, no install scripts, nothing from outside the registry. Your SBOM is ready below.
onboarding.proof.failed: It stopped with an error. Run it again, and if it keeps failing check Operations → Job queue for a job that is still holding the slot.
onboarding.proof.nothingScannedHint: The audit finished but opened no files, so it found nothing — that is not the same as finding nothing wrong. A skip almost always means the clone failed: check the git token on Connections, then run it again.
onboarding.proof.whyProvenNoLine: A deterministic check, not a model's judgement: the file is named, so you can open it and confirm.

deps.artifactsDesc: Two files produced by every audit. Neither needs an LLM key, and both are generated from what the scan actually read.

deps.artifactsEvidenceWhat: The audit as a filing: every SBOM, every finding, the timeline of past runs, and a sha256 of each file — so a third party can check nothing was edited afterwards without trusting us.

deps.artifactsWhyAsk: Who asks for these, and why?
deps.artifactsWhyAskBody: Enterprise customers ask for an SBOM during procurement, and increasingly in the contract. From 11 September 2026 the EU Cyber Resilience Act also requires manufacturers to keep an inventory and to monitor it after release — the evidence pack, with its timeline and hashes, is what turns a stack of separate scans into that record. Current scope: {repos} repositories.

settings.llm.docsEngineHint: The API model answers from the code we send it. mcp.title: Connect an editor over MCP
mcp.subtitle: Claude Code, Cursor and anything else that speaks MCP can query this install directly — your symbol graph, who calls what, the public surface, past reviews.
mcp.step1Body: Issued against your own account, so an editor sees exactly what you see — nothing more.
mcp.copyFailed: Could not copy — your browser blocks the clipboard on insecure origins. Select the text and copy it by hand.
mcp.tokenOnceHint: Copy it now — it is shown once and valid for {days} days. Generating another does not revoke this one.
mcp.whatCanItDo: What can an editor do with this?
mcp.whatCanItDoBody: Read, and only read: search symbols, see who calls what, read the public surface of a module, list deprecations, look at past reviews. It cannot change a policy, register a repository or post a comment — the token is issued without those permissions and cannot be asked for them.
mcp.step2Body: One command in the terminal. Run it in the project you want Celmis available in.
mcp.step3Body: Every other MCP client reads a JSON file. Same three values: the URL, the header, the name.
mcp.whereFileBody: Cursor: .cursor/mcp.json in the project, or ~/.cursor/mcp.json for every project. Claude Code also reads .mcp.json in the project root, which is the one to commit if the whole team should get it. Restart the editor after editing it — most clients read the file once at startup.
mcp.verifyBody: Ask the editor something only Celmis knows. If it answers from the graph rather than from the files open in front of it, the connection is live.
mcp.verifyExample:
Who calls createOrder, across all my repositories?
What is the public API surface of the billing module?
What is deprecated that I still use?
mcp.troubleBody: Three things account for almost all of it. The trailing slash on the URL is required — without it the server answers a redirect the client is not obliged to follow. The token expires; generate a new one and replace it in the file. And if the server answers 503 saying MCP is not configured, an operator has to set MCP_JWT_SECRET and restart — that is a server setting, not something this page can fix.

automation.product.title: What Celmis is
automation.product.index: Celmis connects to your repositories and reads them. It builds an index of what is in each one — the files, the symbols in them, and how those refer to one another — and everything below works from that index rather than from a fresh read of the code.
automation.product.answers: It answers questions about that code, in the language you ask them in and with the files it read attached, and it writes documentation from the same index: module and feature descriptions, integration guides, regenerated when the code moves on.
automation.product.reviews: It reviews pull requests. Agents read the diff together with the surrounding code the index already knows about, so a comment can be about what the change does to the rest of the repository and not only about the lines in it.
automation.product.audits: It audits your dependencies for outdated and vulnerable packages, and produces an SBOM and an evidence pack from the same run — the inventory a machine can read, and the record of where each finding came from.
automation.product.scope: All of it belongs to one workspace: its repositories, its documentation, its findings, its keys. What the models cost while doing any of it is on the Usage page, run by run.
automation.selfHosted.title: Running Celmis on your own models
automation.selfHosted.what: Celmis talks to any OpenAI-compatible server, so the parts of it that call a model can run on one you host yourself — the code and the questions never leave your network.
automation.selfHosted.where: Settings → LLM Configuration: on the card for the part you want to move, choose “{option}” as the provider, paste the base URL your server answers on, and type the model name it serves. Most local servers need no API key.
automation.selfHosted.whereSurfaces: Cards you can point at your own server:
automation.selfHosted.embeddings: Not every part is yours to move. Indexing sends your source code to the embedding server, so the operator pins it in the server environment instead of a workspace admin picking it from a list.

automation.selfHosted.commands: Start a server with one of these:
automation.selfHosted.reindex: Changing the embedding model, or the width of its vectors, needs a full re-index: vectors from two models cannot share one collection.

settings.llm.agents.budgetNote: On some models the thinking tokens are spent from the SAME output budget as the answer — on Gemini 3.x one measurement burned 572 of 613 output tokens on reasoning. That is why the default is {tokens}: when the ceiling is too low the findings array is cut mid-JSON, and the agent reports an unreadable reply rather than a truncation. Lower it only when you know that model's thinking is cheap.
settings.llm.agents.claudeEngineNote: The review engine above is set to Claude Code, which makes one pass on the subscription instead of running the agent pipeline. These settings are kept, but nothing reads them until the engine is switched back to API models.
